title: An older America is improving some prevention measures while care capacity and behavioral-health pressures diverge
source_unit: America's Health Rankings 2026 Senior Report executive brief, synthesizing 56 measures from 25 data sources
geography: United States; adults age 65 and older, state comparisons, and selected demographic groups

older_adult_population.value: more than 61 million people age 65 and older

projected_2040_population.value: more than 78 million people age 65 and older projected by 2040

home_health_workers.value: increased from 62 to 65 per 1,000 adults age 65 and older between 2023 and 2024; 38% above 2016

state_gap.value: 166 per 1,000 in New York versus 17 per 1,000 in Florida in 2024

observations.method: America's Health Rankings synthesis of demographic estimates and workforce measures from 25 data sources.
observations.uncertainty: The population projection and workforce rate do not establish future service adequacy, worker retention, care quality, geographic accessibility, or whether workforce growth matches need.
observations.subgroup: Adults age 65 and older, home-health workers, and states with high or low home-health-worker rates.
observations.counterinterpretation: Workforce growth is meaningful capacity progress even when uneven; state differences may reflect labor markets, service models, reporting, population needs, and rurality rather than simple shortage alone.

geriatric_clinicians.value: increased from 39.9 to 41.5 per 100,000 older adults between September 2024 and September 2025

clinical_state_gap.value: 94.5 per 100,000 in the District of Columbia versus 17.3 per 100,000 in South Dakota

unpaid_support.value: 14.4% of people age 15 and older provided unpaid support or assistance to someone age 65 or older in 2023-2024, statistically unchanged from 14.3% in 2021-2022

observations.method: Report synthesis of clinician workforce and American Time Use Survey-related unpaid-support measures.
observations.uncertainty: Clinician counts do not measure appointment availability, quality, specialty mix, or geographic travel burden; unpaid-support prevalence does not measure intensity, adequacy, or caregiver strain.
observations.subgroup: Older adults, geriatric clinicians, and people providing unpaid support to adults age 65 and older.
observations.counterinterpretation: Stable unpaid-support prevalence can coexist with rising total care demand if the older population grows; it does not by itself show a care gap.

denominator.unit: adults age 65 and older where rate measures apply

drug_deaths.value: increased 38% from 9.9 to 13.7 deaths per 100,000 older adults between 2019-2021 and 2022-2024
drug_deaths.unit: deaths per 100,000 adults age 65 and older

suicide_rate.value: increased 4% from 16.9 to 17.6 deaths per 100,000 older adults between 2019-2021 and 2022-2024
suicide_rate.unit: deaths per 100,000 adults age 65 and older

excessive_drinking.unit: share of adults age 65 and older

age_85_suicide.value: 22.7 deaths per 100,000 among adults age 85 and older in 2023

observations.method: Report synthesis of mortality and behavioral-health indicators from public health data sources.
observations.uncertainty: These are population rates and associations; they do not identify causes, individual trajectories, service access, or the role of isolation, pain, substance availability, income, or care quality.
observations.subgroup: Adults age 65 and older, adults age 85 and older, and older men and women where the report provides comparisons.
observations.counterinterpretation: The divergence from some younger-age trends may reflect age-specific measurement, cohort composition, reporting, survival, or changing diagnosis and treatment patterns rather than a single aging-related mechanism.

denominator.unit: adults age 60 and older for food-insecurity measures

food_insecurity.unit: share of adults age 60 and older

older_adults_food_insecure.value: approximately 6.9 million to 7.4 million adults age 60 and older

snap_reach.value: increased from 82.8 to 86.8 participants per 100 adults age 60 and older living in poverty between 2022 and 2023
snap_reach.unit: participants per 100 older adults in poverty

home_delivered_meals.value: 11.3 recipients per 100 adults age 65 and older with independent-living difficulty in 2024, 27% above 2019
home_delivered_meals.unit: recipients per 100 older adults with independent-living difficulty

observations.method: Report synthesis of food-insecurity, SNAP, and home-delivered-meal measures across different age and eligibility universes.
observations.uncertainty: The measures use different denominators and years; increased program reach does not establish adequate benefit levels, enrollment access, nutritional quality, or resolution of food insecurity.
observations.subgroup: Older adults age 60 and older, older adults in poverty, and adults age 65 and older with independent-living difficulty.
observations.counterinterpretation: Support-program expansion and worsening food insecurity can occur simultaneously if need, prices, housing costs, or benefit adequacy rise faster than reach.

boundary: This record adds an aging-and-capacity trend: the older US population is expanding, care workforces are growing but unevenly, behavioral-health risks are worsening in several measures, and food insecurity persists despite greater program reach. It does not establish causal mechanisms, future care adequacy, individual health trajectories, or program effectiveness.
